rows.label: Array temperature derating factor

rows.why_lo: a derating factor cannot be negative

rows.why_lo: a degradation rate cannot be negative

rows.why_lo: a loss fraction cannot be negative

rows.why_lo: a heater load cannot be negative

rows.label: F10.7 activity band
rows.question: Which activity band does this F10.7 fall in?
rows.why_lo: there are four bands and the lowest is 1. A zero or negative band means the counting started in the wrong place, which would shift every label by one and still look like a valid answer
rows.why_hi: there are four bands and the highest is 4, unbounded above in flux — band 4 holds everything from 170 sfu upward, including the record's largest day at 343. A fifth band means an edge was added without the range being updated

rows.label: Geomagnetic alert threshold
rows.question: At what geomagnetic level does the issuing centre put out an alert?
rows.why_lo: Kp is defined on 0 to 9 and no alert in the record was issued below 4. A value under it would mean an alert on a quiet sky, which the issuing centre has never done in 29 years
rows.why_hi: Kp 9 is the top of the scale; there is nothing above it to alert on. Only three alerts in the record carry a threshold of 9

rows.label: Expected Ap over the mission window
rows.question: What daily planetary Ap should the mission window be expected to sit at?
rows.why_lo: below 1 the level is beneath anything the record holds over a rotation: the quietest of 381 rotations in bundles/solar-weather@2026.09.14 has a mean Ap of 1.48. The bound WAS 0, carrying a reason about DAILY Ap — a single quiet day really is Ap 0 — which is the wrong quantity for this row. A rotation mean of 0 needs 27 consecutive Ap-0 days and the record has never held two
rows.why_hi: above 40 the value exceeds anything the record supports for this quantity, so it is an arithmetic error rather than an active sun. This row is a rotation-scale level, and the largest rotation mean of Ap in the 381 rotations of bundles/solar-weather@2026.09.14 is 36.96; the bound WAS 80, which is more than twice a level the sun has never reached over a rotation

rows.label: Sustained cold Ap to design to
rows.question: What Ap must the design still work at as a sustained level over the mission window, on the low side?
rows.why_lo: Ap floors at zero — a perfectly quiet day is Ap 0 and there is nothing below it. On this row the guard is load-bearing rather than decorative: a symmetric band subtracted from a small centre reaches below zero, and what comes out then is arithmetic rather than sky
rows.why_hi: above 300 the level exceeds the largest daily Ap in the record, 273. A COLD level there means the spread has been added rather than subtracted, which is the one failure this row has that its twin does not

rows.label: Single-day cold Ap to design to
rows.question: How quiet can a single day of Ap be inside the mission window?
rows.why_lo: Ap floors at zero — a perfectly quiet day is Ap 0 and there is nothing below it. This is the row in the subsystem closest to its own floor, seven units clear at the declared window, and the only one where the guard is likely to fire on an ordinary input rather than on a mistake
rows.why_hi: 400 is the top of the Ap index itself; a value above it is not a geomagnetic index at all. On the QUIETEST of the five scenarios a value anywhere near it means a sign is wrong somewhere in the chain above

rows.label: Within-rotation daily Ap drop
rows.question: How far below its own rotation does a single day of Ap fall, at the declared confidence, at the level that rotation sits at?
rows.why_lo: a drop of zero would mean no day ever falls below its rotation mean, which the record contradicts on about half the days it holds; below zero is not a distance, and a negative value here means the tail has been read from the wrong end
rows.why_hi: above 150 the value exceeds anything the record supports for this quantity, so it is an arithmetic error rather than a quiet sky

rows.label: Within-rotation daily Ap spread
rows.question: How far above its own rotation does a single day of Ap reach, at the declared confidence, at the level that rotation sits at?
rows.why_lo: a value below zero is not a spread, and Ap itself floors at zero — a quiet day really is Ap 0
rows.why_hi: above 150 the value exceeds anything the record supports for this quantity, so it is an arithmetic error rather than an active sun

rows.label: Ap design value
rows.question: What daily Ap is this design built to survive?
rows.why_lo: the lowest value this relation can return is 48, at G1. A bound at 40 sits just under it and refuses anything that would design to less than a minor storm, which is not a design case: the record has 1358 days at G1 or above, 47 a year
rows.why_hi: the highest this relation can return is 132, at G3, which is the top of the declared G range. A bound at 140 sits just above it and catches a G level outside the range or a misread table. It does NOT bound the sky: the record's largest daily Ap is 273 and the five-year return level is 158.4, both above this bound, and neither passes through this row

rows.label: Sustained Ap to design to
rows.question: What daily planetary Ap must the design survive as a sustained level over the mission window?
rows.why_lo: Ap floors at zero — a perfectly quiet day is Ap 0 — so a design level below it means a spread has been subtracted rather than added
rows.why_hi: above 300 the level exceeds the largest daily Ap in the record, 273, so a SUSTAINED level there is not a window this tool can model

rows.label: Single-day Ap to design to
rows.question: What daily planetary Ap must the design survive on a single day inside the mission window?
rows.why_lo: Ap floors at zero, so a single-day design level below it means a spread has been subtracted rather than added
rows.why_hi: 400 is the top of the Ap index itself; a value above it is not a geomagnetic index at all, and this row — a sustained level plus a daily excursion — is the one in the subsystem most likely to reach for it

rows.label: Ap rotation-forecast residual spread
rows.question: How much of the next rotation's Ap does the pattern fail to explain?
rows.why_lo: a value below zero is not a spread, and Ap itself floors at zero — a quiet day really is Ap 0
rows.why_hi: above 6 the residual would exceed the standard deviation of the rotation means themselves, so the pattern would be worse than predicting the record's own mean. This row is identical in method to sw_mean_band_spread and takes that row's criterion rather than the vaguer one it carried before: the 381 Ap rotation means of bundles/solar-weather@2026.09.14 have a standard deviation of 4.96, and 6 is that rounded up. The bound WAS 20, which is four times what the record supports for a residual of this quantity

rows.label: Confidence the design band is at
rows.question: What confidence is the design band at — one number both halves of it read?

rows.label: Stated band coverage
rows.question: Does the stated 95 per cent band actually contain the truth 95 per cent of the time?
rows.why_lo: below 0.9 a band sold as 95 per cent would be missing the truth twice as often as it claims, and every margin built on sw_f107_design would be smaller than it reads. That is a defect in the percentile table, not a property of the sky, and it should stop a run
rows.why_hi: a coverage cannot exceed 1. A value at exactly 1 would mean the band was never exceeded in 29 years, which for a 95th percentile would mean the table is far too wide and the design is paying for margin it does not need

rows.label: F10.7 central expectation at a lead
rows.question: Where is F10.7 expected to be by the time the mission is there?
rows.why_lo: the answer is a weighted blend of today's F10.7 and a window mean of the analogue, so it cannot leave the interval between them. The analogue is bounded below by 0.324026 x 193.8580 = 62.8 sfu, its smallest shape on its smallest amplitude, and env_f107 by 60 because below 60 sfu has never been observed; the blend therefore floors at 60
rows.why_hi: env_f107's upper bound is 400, above which the exospheric temperature relation is extrapolated past the largest recorded daily value. The analogue cannot exceed cycle 25's own 81-day peak of 225.1 sfu, and a blend cannot exceed its larger input, so this bound catches a broken weight or a broken table rather than an extreme sky

rows.label: Solar cycle number
rows.question: Which numbered solar cycle is the mission epoch in?
rows.why_lo: the record's first cycle is 23 and it begins mid-cycle, so no epoch this tree allows can sit in an earlier one. A lower number means the counting started in the wrong place
rows.why_hi: the record names three cycles and ends inside the third. 26 is one beyond what the data can place, and the bound exists so that an epoch far enough out to need cycle 27 refuses rather than quietly returning 25

rows.label: Solar cycle phase
rows.question: How far through its solar cycle is the mission epoch?
rows.why_lo: a phase is a fraction of the way through a cycle and cannot be negative. A negative value means the epoch precedes the cycle it was assigned to
rows.why_hi: one is the end of the cycle. Above it the epoch belongs to the next cycle, and this row cannot name it because the record does not contain its start — so it refuses instead of folding round silently

rows.label: Cycle-to-cycle repeatability
rows.question: How much does one solar cycle repeat the shape of the last one?
rows.why_lo: below 0.4 the two stacked cycles would share less than 16 per cent of their variance, which would say the solar cycle has no repeatable shape at all. The measured value is 0.770 for 59 per cent shared, and the asymmetric fast rise and slow decline is present in both cycles, so a value that low means the stacking or the boundaries are wrong rather than the Sun being irregular
rows.why_hi: above 0.95 the two cycles would be near-identical in shape, which the record contradicts: the rms difference between the two phase-stacked curves is 37.7 sfu on a pooled mean near 112, and their peaks differ by 28 per cent. An answer that high means the correlation was taken over too few bins or after a normalisation that removed the disagreement

rows.label: Within-rotation daily drop
rows.question: How far below its own rotation does a single day of F10.7 fall, at the declared confidence, at the level that rotation sits at?
rows.why_lo: a drop of zero would mean no day ever falls below its rotation mean, which the record contradicts on about half the days it holds; below zero is not a distance, and a negative value here means the tail has been read from the wrong end
rows.why_hi: above 120 sfu the departure exceeds the largest single-day excursion in the record in either direction, so a value there is an arithmetic error rather than a quiet sun

rows.label: Within-rotation daily spread
rows.question: How far above its own rotation does a single day of F10.7 reach, at the declared confidence, at the level that rotation sits at?
rows.why_lo: a spread of zero would mean every day equals its rotation mean, which the record contradicts on every day it holds; below zero is not a spread
rows.why_hi: above 120 sfu the departure exceeds the largest single-day excursion in the record, so a value there is an arithmetic error rather than an active sun

rows.label: How long the design Ap lasts
rows.question: How long can the mission be before the record expects to exceed the design Ap?
rows.why_lo: the shortest this relation can return is 0.3370 years, at the G1 bound of Ap 48. A bound at 0.3 sits just under it. A value below would mean a design level under Ap 46, which is beneath anything the G scale calls a storm
rows.why_hi: the longest is 2.6242 years, at the G3 bound of Ap 132, which is the top of the declared G range. A bound at 3 sits just above it. It is NOT a claim that no design survives longer: Ap 207 at G4 would reach 16.4 years, and sw_storm_design_level refuses G4 deliberately rather than this guard forbidding it

rows.label: F10.7 burst duration
rows.question: Once F10.7 goes above the spike threshold, how long does it stay there?
rows.why_lo: a run is at least one day by construction, because a run of zero days is not an event. A value below 1 means the run-finding is broken rather than that events are short
rows.why_hi: the longest run in 29 years is 10 days. A mean above it would exceed every single event the record contains, which no averaging can produce

rows.label: How long one exceedance lasts
rows.question: Once the record goes above the design Ap, how long does it stay there?
rows.why_lo: a run is at least one day by construction. A value below 1 means the run-finding is broken rather than that exceedances are brief
rows.why_hi: the longest run at any design level in 29 years is 5 days, at the G1 bound. A mean above that would exceed every single event the record contains, which no averaging can produce

rows.label: When in the cycle exceedances fall
rows.question: Where in the solar cycle do the exceedances of the design Ap fall?
rows.why_lo: cycle phase runs 0 at minimum to 1 at the next minimum, so 0 is the floor by definition. A median at 0 would mean every exceedance fell on the first day of a cycle
rows.why_hi: 1 is the end of a cycle by the same definition. A median at 1 would mean every exceedance fell on the last day of one

rows.label: Days a year above the design level
rows.question: How many days a year does the record go above the design Ap?
rows.why_lo: the lowest rate this relation can return is 0.284, at the G3 bound of Ap 132. A bound at 0.1 sits under it and catches a table read at the wrong end; it is NOT a claim that no design level is exceeded less often, because a higher bound than G3 is outside the declared G range
rows.why_hi: the highest is 4.65, at the G1 bound of Ap 48. A bound at 6 sits just above it. A rate above 6 days a year would mean the design level had fallen to around Ap 40, which is below anything the G scale defines as a storm and below what sw_ap_design can return

rows.label: F10.7 81-day centred mean
rows.question: What 81-day centred mean F10.7 should a density model be given at the mission epoch?
rows.why_lo: the same floor as env_f107: below 60 sfu has never been observed and no relation reading F10.7 has support there
rows.why_hi: the same ceiling as env_f107: above 400 sfu every consumer of F10.7 is extrapolating. An 81-day mean is smoother than the daily value and the largest binned mean-cycle level is 165.3, so this bound is unreachable by the relation and catches a broken input

rows.label: Sustained cold F10.7 to design to
rows.question: What F10.7 must the design still work at as a sustained level over the mission window, on the low side?
rows.why_lo: below 60 sfu has never been observed and every relation reading F10.7 has no support there. On this row the guard means something specific: a sustained level below the record's own floor says the band is wider than the sky, which happens when a window near solar minimum is given a sigma measured across a whole cycle
rows.why_hi: above 400 sfu the exospheric temperature relation is extrapolated past the largest recorded daily value. A COLD level there is arithmetic rather than sky — it means the spread has been added rather than subtracted, which is the one failure this row has that its twin does not

rows.label: Single-day cold F10.7 to design to
rows.question: How cold can a single day of F10.7 be inside the mission window?
rows.why_lo: below 60 sfu has never been observed and every relation reading F10.7 has no support there. This is the row most likely to reach it — a symmetric rotation band and a daily drop stacked on a low centre — and it DID reach it, until sw_daily_band_drop was conditioned on the rotation level. The guard is here rather than downstream because this is where the impossible number is formed
rows.why_hi: above 400 sfu the exospheric temperature relation is extrapolated past the largest recorded daily value. On the COLDEST of the five scenarios a value there means a sign is wrong somewhere in the chain above it

rows.label: F10.7 to design to
rows.question: What F10.7 should this design be sized to?
rows.why_lo: below 60 sfu has never been observed and every relation reading F10.7 has no support there — env_f107's own floor, and a design value below it means the spread has been subtracted rather than added
rows.why_hi: above 400 sfu the exospheric temperature relation is extrapolated past the largest recorded daily value, which is env_f107's stated reason for the same bound. This guard is reachable: a central expectation near the top of its range plus a fifteen-year spread would exceed it, and it should refuse rather than hand a consumer a flux it cannot model

rows.label: Sustained F10.7 to design to
rows.question: What F10.7 must the design survive as a sustained level over the mission window?
rows.why_lo: below 60 sfu has never been observed and every relation reading F10.7 has no support there; a design level below it means the spread has been subtracted rather than added
rows.why_hi: above 400 sfu the exospheric temperature relation is extrapolated past the largest recorded daily value, and a sustained level there is not a window this tool can model

rows.label: Single-day F10.7 to design to
rows.question: What F10.7 must the design survive on a single day inside the mission window?
rows.why_lo: below 60 sfu has never been observed and every relation reading F10.7 has no support there; a single-day design level below it means a spread has been subtracted rather than added
rows.why_hi: above 400 sfu the exospheric temperature relation is extrapolated past the largest recorded daily value — and this row, being the sustained level plus a daily excursion, is the one most likely to reach it, which is exactly why the guard is here

rows.label: Observed F10.7, the forecast's anchor
rows.by: A. Rai / 2026-09-01, carried unchanged from env_f107
rows.question: What is the 10.7 cm radio flux doing now, for the forecast to start from?
rows.why_lo: the same floor env_f107 declared and for the same reason: below 60 sfu has never been observed and every relation reading F10.7 has no support there
rows.why_hi: the same ceiling env_f107 declared: above 400 sfu is beyond the largest recorded daily value, so anything reading it is extrapolating

rows.label: Daily F10.7 scatter about F10.7A
rows.question: How far does a single day's F10.7 stray from its own 81-day centred mean?
rows.why_lo: below 0.05 the daily flux would sit within five per cent of its 81-day mean on a typical day, which would make the daily driver and the smoothed one interchangeable. The record's 99th percentile ratio is 1.371, so it is not
rows.why_hi: above 0.25 the typical day would be a quarter away from its own baseline and the 81-day mean would not be describing the same quantity as the day. A value there means the window or the pairing is wrong rather than that the Sun is variable

rows.label: Issued-outlook F10.7 bias
rows.question: By how much does the published outlook miss the F10.7 that arrived?
rows.why_lo: the deepest measured bias is -3.968 sfu, at lead 26, the last verifiable lead. A value below -4 means the table was misread or the bundle changed underneath it
rows.why_hi: the shallowest measured bias is -0.593 sfu, at lead 1. A value above -0.5 — and certainly a positive one — would say the outlook over-forecasts F10.7 somewhere in the window, which this record does not show at any lead. The guard is deliberately on the safe side of zero rather than at zero, because an answer of -0.1 sfu would be as wrong as +0.1 and a bound at zero would pass it

rows.label: Issued-outlook skill against persistence
rows.question: Is the published outlook better than assuming today's F10.7 continues?
rows.why_lo: the worst measured skill is -0.036, at lead 24. A bound at -0.1 leaves room for the three negative leads and refuses anything that would say the published outlook is substantially worse than doing nothing, which the record does not support
rows.why_hi: the best measured skill is +0.438, at lead 9. A skill above 0.5 against persistence would mean the outlook halves the baseline's mean squared error, and nothing in this record comes close; an answer there means the table was misread or the bundle changed underneath it

rows.label: F10.7 error from climatology at a lead
rows.question: If we forecast the record's mean F10.7 and nothing else, how wrong are we L days later?
rows.why_lo: an RMS cannot be negative, and this one cannot approach zero: it is the spread of the record about its own mean, which is 44 sfu
rows.why_hi: the measured entries run 44.39 to 45.32 sfu and the relation is a table that clamps, so no input can produce more. 50 is above both and tight enough to catch a broken table, which a bound of 65 would not

rows.label: F10.7 error from persistence at a lead
rows.question: If all we know is today's F10.7, how wrong are we L days later?
rows.why_lo: an RMS cannot be negative. Zero would mean persistence is exact, which is true only at a lead of zero and is not a lead this row is asked about
rows.why_hi: for a memoryless process the structure function saturates at sqrt(2)*sigma, which is 62.77 sfu on this record, and the largest measured entry is 49.63 at a two-year lead. 65 is above both, so it is unreachable by this relation and exists to catch a broken table rather than an extreme sky

rows.label: Kp slot the design is driven by
rows.question: Which Kp slot is the design driven by — the day's mean, or its worst three-hour interval?

rows.label: Kp from daily Ap
rows.question: What Kp does this daily planetary Ap mean?
rows.why_lo: Kp is defined on 0..9 and the table's first point is Kp 0 at ap 0; a negative index is a sign error, not a quiet day
rows.why_hi: Kp is defined on 0..9 and the table's last point is Kp 9 at ap 400. This is the same guard env_kp carries, and it catches an ap value reaching a consumer that wanted Kp

rows.label: Kp slot bias, 24-hour mean
rows.question: By how much does the published table over-read the 24-hour MEAN Kp at this Ap?
rows.why_lo: the deepest measured bin median is -0.487 and the relation is a table that clamps at its ends, so no input can produce less. -1.0 is therefore unreachable by this relation and exists to catch a broken table rather than an extreme sky
rows.why_hi: Jensen's inequality puts this at or below zero wherever the published Ap is the mean of the day's eight ap, and the one bin that measures positive measures +0.042. +0.5 would say the table under-reads the 24-hour mean by half a Kp, which no bin shows and which is the signature of the peak-slot offset having been put in this row by mistake

rows.label: Kp in both slots, for all five scenarios
rows.question: What Kp does each of the five driver scenarios carry, in the mean slot and in the peak slot?
rows.why_lo: Kp is defined on 0 to 9 and the scale's first point is Kp 0 at ap 0; a negative index is a sign error, not a quiet sky
rows.why_hi: Kp is defined on 0 to 9 and the scale's last point is Kp 9 at ap 400. This member is the worst slot of the worst day, so it is the one of the ten most likely to reach it

rows.label: Kp slot bias, daily peak
rows.question: By how much does the published table under-read the daily PEAK Kp at this Ap?
rows.why_lo: Kp(ap) is concave, so by Jensen's inequality the daily peak three-hourly Kp cannot sit below the table's reading of the daily mean. A negative correction contradicts the inequality the whole row rests on, and means the sign or the slot has been swapped. The smallest measured bin median is +0.833
rows.why_hi: the largest measured bin median is +1.747 and the relation is a table that clamps at its ends, so no input can produce more than that. 2.0 is therefore unreachable by this relation and exists to catch a broken table rather than an extreme sky

rows.label: Rotation-forecast residual spread
rows.question: How much of the next rotation's level does the pattern fail to explain?
rows.why_lo: a spread of zero would mean the pattern predicts every rotation exactly, which the record contradicts at every rotation it scores; below zero is not a spread
rows.why_hi: above 45 sfu the residual would exceed the standard deviation of the rotation means themselves, so the pattern would be worse than predicting the record's own mean and the band would be arithmetic rather than physics. The bound WAS 60, which was wider than this same sentence justifies: the 382 rotation means of bundles/solar-weather@2026.09.14 have a standard deviation of 41.45 sfu, and 45 is that rounded up far enough that refreshing the bundle does not move the bound

rows.label: Mean-cycle F10.7 at a phase
rows.question: What F10.7 does the average solar cycle show at this phase?
rows.why_lo: the same floor as env_f107: below 60 sfu has never been observed and no relation reading F10.7 has support there
rows.why_hi: the same ceiling as env_f107: above 400 sfu every consumer of F10.7 is extrapolating. The largest binned mean is 165.3, so this bound is unreachable by the relation and catches a broken table

rows.label: Forecast verification lead
rows.question: At what lead is the published short-term outlook verified?
rows.why_lo: a lead of less than a day is not a forecast the published outlook makes; its first verifiable row is lead 1, present for all 1281 issues
rows.why_hi: 26 is the last lead in the published window that the record can verify, because lead_days is indexed two ways in the same column and only the 1-based minority reaches 27. At 26 the sample is 868 issues drawn from both conventions; at 27 it is 192 drawn from one, and the answer there has a different sign from each of its neighbours. A larger value would be asking the verification rows about a cell whose contents are a property of the indexing rather than of the forecast

rows.label: Rotation recurrence lag
rows.question: At what lag does the solar-rotation signal in F10.7 peak?
rows.why_lo: below 20 days the autocorrelation is still on the steep descent from lag 1 and is falling, not peaking: it reads +0.186 at lag 20 against +0.376 at the peak. A value there would mean the detrending removed the rotation instead of the cycle
rows.why_hi: above 35 days the first bump has closed — the correlation is +0.031 at lag 35 and negative by 36 — and anything beyond is the second harmonic near lag 54, which is the same signal counted twice. A value there would be reporting a harmonic as the fundamental

rows.label: Rotation recurrence strength
rows.question: How strong is the solar-rotation recurrence in F10.7?
rows.why_lo: below 0.1 the rotation bump would be indistinguishable from the noise floor of the detrended series, whose correlation sits between -0.09 and +0.03 across lags 36 to 47. A value there means the detrending removed the signal
rows.why_hi: above 0.7 a rotation-ahead correlation would be stronger than the measured one-day correlation of the same series at lag 5 (+0.531), which would mean F10.7 is more predictable 26 days out than 5 days out. The measured value is 0.376 and nothing in the record approaches 0.7

rows.label: Geomagnetic regime
rows.question: Quiet, active or storm — which regime is this daily Ap in?
rows.why_lo: 1 is quiet and is the lowest regime the mixture defines. Below it there is no label
rows.why_hi: 3 is storm and is the highest. A fourth regime would be a different classifier than the one this row ports

rows.label: Semiannual Ap amplitude
rows.question: How large is the semiannual variation in geomagnetic activity?
rows.why_lo: below 0.5 Ap the seasonal swing would be under 5 per cent of the mean and indistinguishable from the scatter between the record's individual months, whose means range 8.33 to 11.88. A value there means the fit lost the signal
rows.why_hi: above 3.0 Ap the modelled peak-to-trough swing would exceed 6 Ap, more than half the record's mean of 10.5 and larger than the observed spread of the monthly means, which is 3.55 from December to September. An answer that large means an annual or cycle term leaked into the semiannual one

rows.label: F10.7 spike threshold
rows.question: How far above its own 81-day mean must F10.7 rise to count as a spike?
rows.why_lo: below 1.1 the threshold would sit inside one standard deviation of the ratio and catch roughly a fifth of all days. A fifth of the record is not a set of events, it is the weather, and every relation downstream that treats a spike as exceptional would be wrong
rows.why_hi: above 1.6 nothing is caught: the largest ratio in 29 years is 2.109781 and only 30 days exceed 1.5. A threshold there would make the spike rows describe a handful of days and the event duration would be a statistic of three or four bursts

rows.label: Storm level designed for
rows.question: Which NOAA G level is this design built to survive?
rows.why_lo: G1 is the bottom of the NOAA scale. Below it there is no storm to design for — Kp 4 is 'active' and is where alerts begin, which sw_alert_threshold carries, not where storms do
rows.why_hi: G3 is the highest level this vehicle class is sized for. G4 occurs on 49 days in 29 years and G5 on 16, and both are handled by operating through the event rather than by building for it. A design that genuinely requires G4 changes this bound on purpose and re-runs the closure

rows.label: Days a year above a Kp threshold
rows.question: How many days a year does the real sky exceed this Kp?
rows.why_lo: a count of days cannot be negative. Zero is reachable and is the measured value at the top of the scale, which the assumptions say means not observed in 28.2 years rather than impossible
rows.why_hi: there are at most 366 days in a year, so a rate above that is a counting error rather than a sky. The largest measured entry is 364.15 days a year above Kp 0, which is every day the record has an Ap at all

rows.label: Ap at a storm return period
rows.question: What daily planetary Ap recurs once per mission lifetime?
rows.why_lo: ap is an equivalent amplitude in nanotesla. Below 20 the answer is not a storm at all — the record's median day is 7 — so a return level under it means the input or the fit reached somewhere neither was meant to go
rows.why_hi: THE BOUND IS THE RECORD'S LENGTH, NOT THE TABLE'S END. The fit evaluated at a return period equal to the record itself, 28.1971 years, is Ap 229.18; 230 is the first round number above it, so a return period beyond the record refuses instead of answering. The previous bound was 400 — the last point of the published ap/Kp table — which first bites at a return period of 1832 years, sixty-five times the record, and so enforced nothing: this node would answer a once-per-century question with Ap 281 while its own assumptions said a century needs a longer record. Note that 230 is BELOW the record's largest single day, Ap 273: rank 1 sits above the log-linear trend and was deliberately left out of the fitting range, so the fit does not chase it. This bound is the fit's own reach, not the record's extreme

rows.label: F10.7 growth at 95% over a lead
rows.question: By how much can F10.7 rise over a lead this long, at 95% confidence?
rows.why_lo: the 95th percentile of the change in F10.7 over a lead of at least half a year is positive everywhere in this record — the smallest measured is +57 sfu. A negative value means the difference has been taken the wrong way round, which would turn a safety margin into a reduction
rows.why_hi: the largest measured percentile is +115.0 sfu at a fifteen-year lead and the relation is a table that clamps at its ends, so no input can produce more. 120 is unreachable by this relation and exists to catch a broken table rather than an extreme sky

rows.label: F10.7 peak level inside the mission window
rows.question: What is the highest level the cycle analogue reaches during the mission?
rows.why_lo: the analogue's smallest value anywhere is its smallest shape on its smallest amplitude, 0.324026 x 193.8580 = 62.8 sfu, and a maximum over any window is at least that. 60 is env_f107's floor, below which no F10.7 has been observed, so an answer under it means the shape table or an amplitude has been corrupted rather than that the Sun is quiet
rows.why_hi: the analogue's largest value anywhere is 1.000000 x 225.1358 = 225.1 sfu, cycle 25's own 81-day peak, because the shape is normalised to one at a cycle maximum. 400 is env_f107's ceiling and is unreachable by this relation; it catches a broken amplitude rather than an extreme sky

rows.label: Mission duration
rows.question: How long must the mission operate?
rows.why_lo: below six months the programme cannot amortise a satellite, so it is not the mission being designed
rows.why_hi: above 15 years the cost model, the degradation model and the battery cycle model are all extrapolated well past their fits

rows.label: Mission epoch
rows.question: On what date does the mission begin?
rows.why_lo: day 6575 is 2018-01-01. A mission epoch before it would sit inside the archive rather than ahead of the design, and every forward-looking row would be answering a question about the past while presenting it as a prediction
rows.why_hi: day 14610 is 2040-01-01. Beyond it the cycle-phase rows would be folding the phase through more than one unobserved cycle, and the mean cycle length they fold with is measured from two complete cycles. Extrapolating a 11.4-year mean across fifteen years is not a design input, it is a guess with a date on it

rows.label: Ap, sustained
rows.question: What geomagnetic index does the system design to, as a level sustained over the mission?
rows.why_lo: the crossing's own floor, restated. A row that narrowed the range it received would be changing the answer while appearing to relay it
rows.why_hi: the crossing's own ceiling, restated. This is a single-day value, so it is the one most likely of the pair to approach it

rows.label: F10.7, sustained daily value
rows.question: What daily F10.7 does the system design to, on the scenario it sits in?
rows.why_lo: the crossing's own floor, restated. A row that narrowed the range it received would be changing the answer while appearing to relay it
rows.why_hi: the crossing's own ceiling, restated. This is a single-day value, so it is the one most likely of the pair to approach it

rows.label: F10.7, 81-day mean
rows.question: What 81-day mean F10.7 does the single-day design value ride on?
rows.why_lo: the crossing's own floor, restated: an 81-day mean cannot sit below a floor every day of it respects
rows.why_hi: the crossing's own ceiling, restated: above 400 sfu every consumer of F10.7 is extrapolating

rows.label: Kp, worst slot of the sustained day
rows.question: What Kp does the system design to, in the worst three-hour slot of its design day?
rows.why_lo: the crossing's own floor, restated: Kp is defined on 0 to 9 and a negative index is a sign error, not a quiet sky
rows.why_hi: the crossing's own ceiling, restated: Kp is defined on 0 to 9. This member is the worst slot of the worst day, so it is the one of the ten nearest it — 8.00 at the declared window

rows.label: Solar flux, sustained
rows.question: What solar flux does the system design to, as a level sustained for months at a time?
rows.why_lo: the crossing's own floor, restated: below 60 sfu has never been observed and every relation reading F10.7 has no support there. A row that narrowed the range it received would be changing the answer
rows.why_hi: the crossing's own ceiling, restated: above 400 sfu the exospheric temperature relation is extrapolated past the largest recorded daily value

rows.label: Absorbed albedo
rows.question: How much reflected sunlight off the Earth does the spacecraft absorb?
rows.why_lo: absorbed power cannot be negative
rows.why_hi: above 100 kW the illuminated area is not this spacecraft

rows.label: Absorbed Earth infrared
rows.question: How much of the Earth's own thermal emission does the spacecraft absorb?
rows.why_lo: absorbed power cannot be negative
rows.why_hi: above 100 kW the surface is not this spacecraft

rows.label: Absorbed direct solar
rows.question: How much heat does direct sunlight put into the spacecraft?
rows.why_lo: absorbed power cannot be negative
rows.why_hi: above 100 kW the illuminated area is not this spacecraft

rows.label: Solar absorptivity
rows.question: What fraction of incident sunlight does the external surface absorb?
rows.why_lo: below 0.05 no space-qualified coating is that reflective after atomic-oxygen exposure
rows.why_hi: unity is a perfect black body, the limit rather than a coating

rows.label: Free-molecular aerodynamic heating
rows.question: How much does the air itself heat the spacecraft?
rows.why_lo: heating cannot be negative
rows.why_hi: above 100 kW the vehicle is re-entering

rows.label: Heat to reject
rows.question: How much heat does the spacecraft have to get rid of?
rows.why_lo: heat to reject cannot be negative
rows.why_hi: above 50 kW nothing in this mass class dissipates that much

rows.label: Infrared emissivity
rows.question: How well does the external surface radiate in the infrared?
rows.why_lo: below 0.05 the surface cannot reject heat at all and no design closes
rows.why_hi: unity is a perfect emitter, the limit rather than a coating

rows.label: Equilibrium temperature
rows.question: What temperature does the spacecraft settle at?
rows.why_lo: below 100 K the spacecraft would be colder than deep space plus the Earth's infrared, which is not possible in this orbit
rows.why_hi: above 1000 K nothing survives and the balance is being fed a nonsense load

rows.label: Internal dissipation
rows.question: How much of the electrical power ends up as heat inside the spacecraft?
rows.why_lo: dissipation cannot be negative
rows.why_hi: above 20 kW nothing in this mass class dissipates that much

rows.label: Thermal margin
rows.question: Is the spacecraft inside its temperature limit?
rows.why_lo: a margin below -500 K means the balance is being fed a nonsense load
rows.why_hi: a margin above 500 K means the limit is not the one that binds

rows.label: Radiator area
rows.question: How much area is available to reject heat?
rows.why_lo: below 0.1 m2 no useful heat is rejected
rows.why_hi: above 30 m2 the radiator is the spacecraft

rows.label: Radiator area required
rows.question: How much radiator would be needed to hold the temperature limit?
rows.why_lo: a required area cannot be negative
rows.why_hi: above 1000 m2 the design does not close and the answer is that the dissipation is wrong

rows.label: Upper temperature limit
rows.question: What is the highest temperature the electronics may reach?
rows.why_lo: below 273 K no electronics box in this design is qualified to operate
rows.why_hi: above 400 K no electronics box in this design survives

rows.label: Earth view factor
rows.question: How much of the sky, from a nadir-facing surface, is filled by the Earth?
rows.why_lo: a view factor cannot be negative
rows.why_hi: a view factor cannot exceed one
